how_read: scripts/kb/fetch_wiki_live_pages.py with its page-render call asking for the page by title (this wiki answers HTTP 403 to the reader's 'oldid' form; the scratch wrapper checks that the revision the wiki rendered is the revision the reader resolved, and stops if they differ). Page text as rendered by the wiki, link markup removed. Every quoted sentence below was checked, by script, to appear word for word in the page text read at the revision named (table cell markers removed, whitespace collapsed). Several SmashWiki pages cover the whole series; a line states a Super Smash Bros. (Nintendo 64) fact only where the page says so for the original game, for Smash 64, or sits on a page for a stage or fighter that exists only in the original game.

lines.line: Summary: A healing item that takes damage off whoever grabs it. The first game just calls it Heart, and there it wipes out all of your damage, down to 0%.

quoted: known simply as Heart in the original Super Smash Bros., is an item that will reduce the damage of the character who picks it up
recovering damage all the way down to 0%

lines.line: Uses: It appears in the air and drifts down slowly, which in the first game leaves a gap in which fighters battle over its landing spot. After someone has taken it, the healing carries on even if they are hit during it.

quoted: They spawn above the ground and float down slowly, creating a delay before they land.
in the original Super Smash Bros. players must fight for the area where it will land as it falls.
(even if the player is hit during this time)

lines.line: Tips: Collect enough of them in a single match for the Heartthrob bonus, which pays 17,000 points in the first game and 8,000 in its Japanese release.

quoted: gives the player the Heartthrob bonus, worth 17,000 points in SSB (8,000 points in the Japanese version of SSB)

lines.line: Summary: A red tomato marked with a black M, which takes damage off whoever picks it up. In the first game it clears 100% of your damage; the later games only clear 50%.

quoted: which reduces the damage percentage of the player who picks it up
a red tomato with a black "M" in the center
In Super Smash Bros., the Maxim Tomato restores 100% from a character's damage percentage.
In the Super Smash Bros. games, with the exception of the original game, Maxim Tomatoes only restore fifty percent of a player's damage

lines.line: Uses: In the first game, hits you take during the healing do no damage. Hyrule Castle never gets Maxim Tomatoes.

quoted: In SSB, any damage the character takes is ignored while healing.
Maxim Tomatoes don't spawn on Hyrule Castle.

lines.line: Tips: Eat enough of them in one match for the Vegetarian bonus: 9,000 points in the first game, 5,000 in its Japanese release. Turn off every item but the Maxim Tomato and the containers that drop onto the stage will hold nothing.

quoted: gives the player the Vegetarian bonus, worth 9,000 points in SSB (5,000 points in the Japanese version of SSB)
If all items aside from the Maxim Tomato are turned off, then any containers that fall onto the stage will be empty.

lines.line: Summary: A star that bounces around and gives whoever touches it ten seconds of invincibility. It was called the Starman in the first game, and kept that name until Brawl's PAL release and Smash 4's NTSC release.

quoted: makes whoever it touches invulnerable to all damage and knockback for a short time.
known as the Starman prior to the PAL release of Super Smash Bros. Brawl and the NTSC release of Super Smash Bros. 4
The player's fighter will become invincible for ten seconds

lines.line: Uses: It hops across the stage in big arcs, rebounding from platforms and walls, and it can drop off the edge if nobody catches it soon enough. Touching an enemy while invincible does them no harm. The fighter glitters, and a dedicated tune takes over from the stage music until the effect ends.

quoted: The Super Star bounces on the field and off platforms or walls in large arcs, and can fall off the stage if not grabbed in time
but it doesn't damage the opponents when touched
bright, sparkling appearance
special music theme which completely replaces the stage music

lines.line: Tips: In the first game every item carries a little triangle above it except this one. In the series, invincibility does not save a fighter who falls off the stage: they can still be KO'd.

quoted: In Smash 64, items (except for Super Stars) have a small triangular indicator above them.
Users can still be KO'd if they fall off the stage with it.

lines.line: Summary: A sword modelled on the lightsaber, and nicknamed after it, that you swing for stronger hits or throw at opponents. Among the battering items, it travels the farthest when thrown.

quoted: the Beam Sword will bolster the player's power
It is similar in appearance to a lightsaber, and is often informally referred to as the "lightsaber" for this reason.
it can be wielded and charged for melee attacks or can be thrown, like all other battering items.
It also has the longest range of all Clobbering Items when thrown.

lines.line: Uses: Holding it turns your forward smash, dash attack, forward tilt and neutral attack into item swipes. In the first game they deal 25%, 16%, 18% and 12%, in that order.

quoted: Battering items are wielded by characters once picked up, turning their neutral attack, forward tilt, dash attack, and forward smash into an item swipe.
from the table (first-game column): Neutral Attack 12%
from the table (first-game column): Forward Tilt 18%
from the table (first-game column): Dash Attack 16%
from the table (first-game column): Forward Smash 25%

lines.line: Tips: A thrown Beam Sword deals from 13% to 20%, depending on which throw. Getting hit while you hold it can make you drop it: in the first game the odds are the hit's damage over 60, so a hit of 6% gives a 10% chance.

quoted: from the table (first-game column): Forward tilt throw 15%
from the table (first-game column): Up tilt throw 16%
from the table (first-game column): Down tilt throw 13%
from the table (first-game column): Dash attack throw 19%
from the table (first-game column): Forward smash throw 19%
from the table (first-game column): Up smash throw 20%
from the table (first-game column): Down smash throw 13%
from the table (first-game column): Air up smash throw 20%
In Smash 64 and Melee, the formula is base damage / 60, so for example, an attack that deals 6% damage has a 10% chance of causing the target to drop their held item

lines.line: Summary: A wooden bat that changes your forward smash: you wind up and take one slow swing, which can knock an opponent out with a single hit.

quoted: completely altering the character's forward smash. Upon performing a forward smash, the character winds up and performs a single, delayed swing that can potentially KO opponents in a single hit.
is that of a traditional wooden bat with a striped tip and a wrapped handle

lines.line: Uses: Each swing takes the same amount of time, and you cannot charge it. In the first game it reuses each fighter's ordinary item swing, so the wind-up depends on who you play: Link needs only 23 frames, while Mario, Luigi and Ness need the most, at 30.

quoted: The attack always takes a set amount of time and cannot be charged
In Smash 64 and Melee, characters use their standard item swinging animation
In Smash 64 and Melee, swing time varies from character to character, but is much faster overall than in later games.
from the table (first-game column): SSB Mario 30 Donkey Kong 28 Link 23 Samus 26 Yoshi 27 Kirby 26 Fox 29 Pikachu 27 Luigi 30 Ness 30 Captain Falcon 28 Jigglypuff 26

lines.line: Tips: Hit with the end of the bat for the most damage, not the centre. Thrown, it is also strong, around 20% with big knockback, and ordinary swings can KO fairly early, above all a dash attack or a smash throw.

quoted: The Home-Run Bat deals most of its damage at the tip of the bat instead of the center
The Bat is also powerful when thrown, dealing around 20% damage and high knockback.
the Home-Run Bat is also powerful when swung or thrown normally, being capable of KOing relatively early, especially in regards to its dash attack and smash throws.

lines.line: Summary: A short-range item: its holder keeps swinging it to and fro, and in the first game every hit does 30% with very high knockback.

quoted: is a close-range item that appears in all Super Smash Bros. games.
it sends them into a unique state that inflicts significant damage and knockback.
the effects of the Hammer are even more formidable in Super Smash Bros., where the Hammer instead does 30% damage with even more knockback.

lines.line: Uses: In the series, holding it means you swing without pause and cannot use an air jump, any other attack or a shield. You cannot discard it by choice; only being knocked into a tumble makes you let go. The wiki says it can also follow up on itself for 60%, which will likely KO.

quoted: they will constantly swing the hammer back and forth, and will be unable to midair jump, use any other attacks, or defend.
The Hammer also cannot be manually dropped unless the user has been sent into a state of tumbling.
The Hammer can also "chain" into itself, doing 60% and likely KOing the opponent.

lines.line: Tips: The item list names it among the items to fear most, because of its reach, damage and knockback. Still, in the series the person holding it has no special moves or air jump, so sending them off a ledge mid-swing can KO them. Carefully placed hitboxes can also cut the swing short.

quoted: One of the most feared items in the game due to its range, damage, and knockback.
As the wielder of the hammer cannot use special moves or midair jump, sending an opponent off a ledge while they swing the Hammer can effectively KO them unless they can somehow drop the Hammer.
particularly careful hitbox placement by other characters can potentially interrupt the wielder.

lines.line: Summary: A long-range laser gun with room for 16 shots. In the first game each shot deals 10% electric damage and knocks the target vertically.

quoted: A Ray Gun can be shot 16 times before it runs out of ammunition.
In the original Super Smash Bros. the shots deal 10% electric damage per shot, vertical knockback, and can be fired every 30 frames.

lines.line: Uses: You can fire one shot each 30 frames. Like the other shooting items it usually takes over your neutral attack, and when its ammo runs out it fires only blanks. The item list adds that its blasts have unlimited horizontal range.

quoted: can be fired every 30 frames.
Fires blasts of energy that have infinite horizontal range.
Shooting items fire projectiles when used, typically replacing the neutral attack and neutral aerial of the user. They all have limited ammunition and will merely shoot blanks once it runs out.

lines.line: Tips: A reflect or absorb move can handle the shots, while the gun itself can be reflected only when thrown. In the first two Smash games a fighter had to stand still while using a shooting item; Brawl was when firing on the move became possible.

quoted: The shots can be reflected or absorbed, while the gun itself (when thrown) can only be reflected.
Starting in Brawl, (along with other shooting items) the Ray Gun can be fired while walking.
While characters could not move while using the item in the first two games, shooting items were later changed in Brawl as to allowing running and jumping while shooting such items

lines.line: Summary: A bomb on two stubby legs with a wind-up key sticking out of its back. Its blast does heavy damage and knockback, and it can catch the thrower too.

quoted: They are bomb-like enemies with simple eyes that feature two little legs and a wind-up key on the back.
Being an explosive, the item can easily inflict large damage and knockback to other players, but it can also potentially harm the attacker.
When grabbed and thrown at an enemy, this item explodes, but if left alone, it will start walking around until its timer reaches zero

lines.line: Uses: Pick it up and throw it at an opponent. The thrower can be hurt too, and any attack that hits it sets it off.

quoted: Bob-ombs can be picked up by any player and subsequently thrown at opponents.
Bob-ombs also explode if they are simply hit by an attack.
but it can also potentially harm the attacker.

lines.line: Tips: If nobody grabs it, the game's manual says it wanders off until its countdown reaches zero. In the series it then gets to its feet and paces to and fro along the platform where it appeared, turning at the edges; it goes off if it bumps into a fighter, and otherwise detonates by itself after a while.

quoted: if left alone, it will start walking around until its timer reaches zero

If a Bob-omb is not picked up, after a while, it will stand up and begin to walk back and forth on the platform it spawned on, turning around at edges. In this state, it will explode if it walks into a player.
If it doesn't meet a character it will blow itself up after a while.

lines.line: Summary: The 1P Game's final boss, met in stage 11 on Final Destination. Knocking it past the edge of the stage does not clear the stage; only wearing down its 300 hit points does.

quoted: The final stage takes place at the Final Destination
it can not be cleared by knocking the opponent out past the blast line, but only by reducing the opponent's stamina to 0 HP.
Master Hand on all difficulties has 300 HP.

lines.line: Weak points: No amount of knockback KOs Master Hand, and he is not pushed back by your hits, so draining his 300 hit points is the only way to win.

quoted: receives no knockback from the player's attacks.
Master Hand cannot be defeated by being launched out of the blast zones. Instead, he has 300 hit points that must be depleted.

lines.line: Looks like: A big hand in a glove.

quoted: resembling a large, gloved hand

lines.line: Tips: Side Punch is a fist that drives across the stage for 20%. Big Swipe is a wide slap over the platform for 16%. Floor Sweep makes several passes over the stage at 12% per swipe. Power Punch hangs above you, then slams down in a burst of electricity. Below 100 HP, his Finger Bullet fires three pairs of Bullet Bills instead of one pair.

quoted: from the table (first-game page): Side Punch (サイドパンチ) 20%
Master Hand makes a fist and punches horizontally across the stage.
from the table (first-game page): Big Swipe (ビッグスワイプ) 16%
Master Hand makes a wide slapping motion across the platform.
from the table (first-game page): Floor Sweep (床の掃除) 12% per swipe
Master Hand sweeps across the stage several times, depending on the length of the platform.
Master Hand hovers over the target, then quickly punches down with electric effects.
Master Hand makes the shape of a gun, and fires a pair of Bullet Bills. If Master Hand has less than 100 HP remaining, he will fire three pairs.

lines.line: Summary: A sub-boss of the 1P Game's ninth stage, found solely on the Meta Crystal level. Few attacks make him flinch, he shrugs off grabs and throws while his damage is low, and his own hits knock you back unusually far.

quoted: Metal Mario debuts as a sub-boss in Stage 9 of the 1P Game, fought exclusively on the Meta Crystal stage.
rarely flinches from standard attacks (never doing so at low damage percentages), resists grabs and throws at low percentages
While his attacks deal standard damage, they inflict noticeably increased knockback.

lines.line: Weak points: He resists launching until he has taken around 200% (this changes with difficulty), yet edge-guarding him works very well: once he is off the stage his huge falling speed wrecks his recovery. His 8-frame jumpsquat also makes his aerial attacks slow.

quoted: allows him to withstand roughly 200% damage before becoming susceptible to being launched, though this threshold scales with the chosen difficulty setting.
Metal Mario is exceptionally vulnerable to edge-guarding; once knocked offstage, his extreme falling speed severely impairs his recovery
an 8-frame jumpsquat makes aerial attacks sluggish for Metal Mario to execute.

lines.line: Looks like: A quick look makes him seem like Mario in a different outfit.

quoted: he visually resembles an alternate costume of Mario at first glance

lines.line: Tips: He does not dash and seldom jumps; he just walks steadily back and forth over the stage. On low difficulties he stays passive and tends to attack only after being interrupted, and he grows more aggressive and knocks harder as the setting rises. His behaviour is basic: mostly strolling left and right with an occasional attack.

quoted: Metal Mario never dashes and rarely jumps, instead pacing across the stage at a steady walk. On lower difficulties, he acts passively and attacks infrequently, typically only when he is interrupted. Metal Mario's aggression and knockback increase on higher settings.
His AI is very simple, largely just walking left and right and occasionally attacking.

lines.line: Summary: A giant Donkey Kong that you meet in the 1P Game's sixth stage, on Congo Jungle, where two normal-sized computer partners help you fight.

quoted: The sixth stage takes place in Congo Jungle and pits the player against Giant Donkey Kong.
the player is given two regular-sized AI partners to help out.

lines.line: Weak points: He can absorb up to about 300% before he can be launched, and his own hits knock harder and reach farther thanks to his size. That size also makes him an easier target, and his AI can be gamed into pacing along the top platform, although your partners often spoil the pattern by jumping into or attacking him.

quoted: he has a handicap that allows him to sustain up to around 300% before being possible to launch, while having buffed knockback himself.
his own attacks have increased knockback capable of KOing opponents more easily on top of having increased range due to his size

It is possible to exploit Giant DK's AI, making him walk back and forth on the top platform, similar to Metal Mario along with his size making him a larger target to attacks. However, it is harder due to AI partners jumping into him or attacking him which will often interfere with his pattern.

lines.line: Looks like: A Donkey Kong model scaled up to a far bigger size.

quoted: Donkey Kong with a significantly larger model

lines.line: Tips: Look after your partners. If neither is KO'd you get the DK Defender bonus (10,000 points, 7,000 in the Japanese release), and if neither takes any damage you get the DK Perfect bonus (50,000 points). Higher difficulties make him play more like a level 9 computer fighter, while your partners stay at lower levels.

quoted: Defeating Giant Donkey Kong without either teammate being KO'd nets the DK Defender bonus, worth 10,000 points (7,000 points in the Japanese version).
Defeating him without either teammate being damaged at all earns the DK Perfect bonus, worth 50,000 points.
On higher difficulties, Giant DK behaves more similarly to a level 9 CPU while the player's partners are lower in level.

lines.line: Summary: Thirty feeble purple polygon duplicates of the twelve fighters, met in stage 10 of the 1P Game on Duel Zone, with at most three on screen together.

quoted: The tenth stage takes place on Duel Zone and pits the player against the Fighting Polygon Team, consisting of 30 lightweight Fighting Polygons, weak copies of the twelve playable characters.
fighting at most three at any one time

lines.line: Weak points: Being light, they usually fall to one hit, although higher difficulties make them heavier and tougher. Having no special moves cripples their recovery, and they cannot grab. They are passive too: mostly wandering the platforms and hardly ever attacking.

quoted: Due to their low weight, they can usually be defeated in a single blow, but the Polygons get heavier and stronger at higher difficulty levels
these clones cannot use special moves, which impair their recovery, nor can they grab opponents.
they are relatively passive on all difficulties, spending most of their time just walking around the various platforms of the stage, rarely following the player, and very rarely using attacks.

lines.line: Looks like: Angular, glossy purple figures that for the most part follow the outline of the fighter they copy.

quoted: they appear as blocky, shiny purple figures that mostly retain the shape of their respective fighter

lines.line: Tips: They collect items, and a throwing item usually gets thrown right away. In the bonus stage Race to the Finish they turn far more aggressive, chasing you as far as they can and attacking when you are within reach, and you cannot beat them there, nor can they KO you.

quoted: but they will pick up items. Normally, they will use a throwing item as soon as they have picked it up
They are much more aggressive on this stage, chasing the player as far as possible, and attacking whenever they are within reach.
neither can they be defeated nor can they KO the player

lines.line: Summary: Hyrule Castle, the stage where the 1P Game's first opponent Link waits, has four tornadoes that appear at random places; anyone they catch gets flung upward.

quoted: The only terrain effect are the four tornadoes, commonly called "nados" or the "nado" in the Smash 64 community, which spawn randomly over the stage.
In Super Smash Bros., it is the first stage in 1P Game, and Link is the first to be fought.
thrown upward

lines.line: Weak points: A fighter inside a tornado can still be attacked. Land an aerial the moment they come out, and a meteor smash can drive them back in for more damage.

quoted: It is possible to attack someone while they are in a tornado as well, and it is possible to hit the opponent with an aerial when they are released, including a meteor smash to knock opponents back into a tornado to rack up more damage.

lines.line: Tips: A tornado lasts roughly 10 to 20 seconds and wanders in a random direction, and it can abruptly accelerate and chase a fighter. Anyone caught is held for around two seconds, then flung up, which KOs somewhere from 65% to 130%, depending on weight and where the tornado is. In the 1P Game, a tornado KO on Link gives the Tornado Clear bonus of 3,000 points.

quoted: They tend to last around 10-20 seconds, and move randomly in a direction, although they may suddenly speed up and home in on a character.
a character is held for about two seconds before being dealt 14% /18% and thrown upward, KOing between 65% and 130% depending on weight of character and location of the tornado.
Having Link KO'd by a Tornado stage hazard will net the player the Tornado Clear bonus, worth 3,000 points.

lines.line: Summary: Planet Zebes, where the 1P Game's eighth stage pits you against Samus, has acid that keeps rising and falling beneath it. Contact deals damage and heavy knockback, which can KO a fighter who already has high damage.

quoted: The eighth stage takes place on Planet Zebes and pits the player against Samus.
Touching the acid results in damage and high knockback, capably KOing a player if their damage meter is high.
Its environment rapidly changes due to the rising and falling acid.

lines.line: Weak points: The acid never climbs as far as the highest platform. A fighter knocked into it is shot upward, which gives a chance to use the recovery again, or to just drop back to the stage.

quoted: though never rising high enough to reach the topmost platform.
in the event a player is knocked off the stage and into the acid, it will launch them skyward, allowing them to reuse their recovery or simply fall back onto the stage.

lines.line: Tips: Holding a Starman, or anything else that strongly resists knockback, protects you from the acid; but if you drop past the stage's edge and into it while invincible, you self-destruct. Samus KO'd by the acid earns the Acid Clear bonus: 1,500 points (1,000 in the Japanese release).

quoted: Obtaining a Starman (or any form of strong knockback resistance) grants invulnerability to the acid
if, while invincible, the player falls off the stage and through the acid, they will self-destruct
Having Samus KO'd by the rising acid stage hazard will net the player the Acid Clear bonus, worth 1,500 points (1,000 points in the Japanese version).

lines.line: Summary: On Sector Z, where the 1P Game's third stage has you face Fox, Arwings sweep past and shoot lasers over the stage, dealing big damage and knockback.

quoted: Arwing fighters will occasionally fire at the players, dealing large amounts of damage and knockback.
In the 1P Game, the player fights Fox on this stage.
Fox's favourite ship, Arwing, flies past and indiscriminately shoots its lasers across the stage.
The third stage takes place in Sector Z and pits the player against Fox.

lines.line: Tips: Standing on an Arwing is risky: if it leaves the screen over the top or the side, you can be KO'd, and since Arwings often barrel roll or fly inverted, they effectively throw you off. You cannot stand on the Great Fox's main guns, and they never fire. Knocking Fox out with an Arwing earns the ARWING Clear bonus: 4,000 points (3,000 in the Japanese release). Sector Z is the biggest stage in the game.

quoted: Having Fox KO'd by an Arwing stage hazard will net the player the ARWING Clear bonus, worth 4,000 points (3,000 points in the Japanese version).
Sector Z is the largest stage in Super Smash Bros.

a character standing on a fighter may be KO'd if the fighter flies offscreen to the top or side; however, the Arwings do tend to barrel roll or fly upside down, which essentially pushes the character off.
the main guns of the Great Fox cannot be stood on and do not fire.
